options.text: Upande ambao kwa kawaida uko juu kwenye ramani
Upande wa jua linapotua jioni
options.misconception: Anachanganya kaskazini na magharibi, ambapo jua hutua.

options.text: Upande ulio chini kwenye ramani ya Kenya
options.misconception: Anachanganya kaskazini na kusini kwa kuamini upande wa chini ndio wa kaskazini.

proposed.rationale: Kwenye ramani, kaskazini kwa kawaida huwa juu, na neno hili hutafutwa kwenye kamusi au mtandaoni kama maana ya mada lengwa.

options.text: Kuchagua tovuti yenye picha nyingi za rangi kali
options.misconception: Anafikiri picha nyingi zenye rangi ndizo ishara ya tovuti inayofaa kwa kusoma.

Kuchagua tovuti ambayo marafiki zake wengi wanaitumia

options.misconception: Anafikiri tovuti zenye matangazo ya kuvutia ndizo zinazofaa kwa kujifunza kusoma.

runs.sub_strand: 3.1 Aspects of Traditional Culture in the County

proposed.question: Which one is an aspect of traditional culture in our county?

options.text: A computer in the school library
options.misconception: Believes culture only includes modern items brought in from outside the county.

options.text: The local food cooked for weddings
The electricity bill paid each month
options.misconception: Thinks any regular household expense counts as part of traditional culture.

options.text: The motorbikes used for taxi rides in town
options.misconception: Thinks anything commonly used in daily life in the county counts as culture.

proposed.rationale: Local food cooked for special occasions is a traditional aspect of culture, listed in the curriculum as food.
proposed.excerpt: identify aspects of traditional culture in the County

proposed.question: Which of these is a traditional festival or ceremony?

options.text: The national Independence Day parade
options.misconception: Thinks national public holidays are the same as traditional community festivals.

options.text: The football match held on Saturday
options.misconception: Believes any sport played today is a traditional sport or game.

options.text: The harvest celebration of the community
The market day when shops sell goods
options.misconception: Thinks everyday trading activities are traditional ceremonies.

proposed.rationale: A harvest celebration held by a community is a traditional festival or ceremony.
proposed.excerpt: festivals and ceremonies

proposed.question: Traditional houses in many parts of Kenya are often built using which materials?

options.text: Mud, grass and sticks
Steel and glass only
options.misconception: Believes traditional housing must be made of modern materials.

options.text: Bricks and cement from a factory
options.misconception: Thinks modern building materials are the traditional way to build houses.

options.text: Plastic sheets and metal tiles
options.misconception: Assumes that any roof or wall material used today is part of traditional housing.

proposed.rationale: Many traditional houses in Kenya were built from natural local materials such as mud, grass and sticks.
proposed.excerpt: describe aspects of traditional culture in the County.

proposed.question: Why do communities keep their traditional songs and dances alive?

options.text: Because they are old and no longer useful
options.misconception: Believes old cultural practices lose their value and should be dropped.

options.text: Because the government requires them at every school
options.misconception: Thinks culture is only kept because of laws or rules from outside the community.

options.text: So that children will forget the old ways
options.misconception: Believes culture should be abandoned rather than passed on.

options.text: To pass on values, history and identity to children

proposed.rationale: Traditional songs and dances carry the community's values, history and identity from one generation to the next.
proposed.excerpt: appreciate the importance of traditional culture in the County

proposed.question: Which best explains why traditional culture is important in a county?

options.text: It makes the county's roads and buildings stronger
options.misconception: Thinks culture is about physical structures rather than people's identity.

options.text: It helps people know who they are and where they come from
It is only needed by elders and not by young people
options.misconception: Believes culture matters only to older people and not to the young.

options.text: It replaces the need for schools and hospitals
options.misconception: Thinks culture can take the place of modern public services.

proposed.rationale: Traditional culture gives people a sense of identity, belonging and connection to their community's past.
proposed.excerpt: discuss the importance of traditional culture in the County.

proposed.question: Which of these is a form of child abuse in the community?

options.text: Helping a child to read homework each night
options.misconception: Believes any adult help or attention given to a child counts as abuse.

options.text: Forcing a girl to marry before she grows up
Taking children to the clinic for check-ups
options.misconception: Believes that caring for a child's health is a form of harm.

options.text: Letting children play games with friends outside
options.misconception: Believes that giving children free time to play is a harmful practice.

proposed.rationale: Forcing a girl to marry early is early and forced marriage, which is a form of child abuse listed in the curriculum.
proposed.excerpt: brainstorm forms of child abuse in the community

proposed.question: Which cultural practice violates the rights of children?

options.text: Cutting the private parts of girls for tradition
Children sharing folk stories by the fire at night
options.misconception: Believes that any traditional cultural activity involving children is harmful.

options.text: Elders blessing children during a family ceremony
options.misconception: Believes that elders giving blessings to children is a violation of their rights.

options.text: Families singing traditional songs at harvest time
options.misconception: Believes that all traditional songs and celebrations hurt children.

proposed.rationale: Female genital mutilation is a harmful cultural practice that violates child rights.
proposed.excerpt: use digital or print resources to identify cultural practices that violate child rights in the community

proposed.question: Which is an effect of child abuse on a child?

options.text: Getting better marks in class each term
options.misconception: Believes that abuse can help a child to perform better in school.

options.text: Feeling afraid and finding it hard to learn
Making many new friends at school quickly
options.misconception: Believes that abused children become more social and confident.

options.text: Having more free time to play outside
options.misconception: Believes that abuse gives children more freedom and leisure.

proposed.rationale: Child abuse often leaves children feeling afraid and makes it hard for them to learn and concentrate.
proposed.excerpt: discuss effects of child abuse in the community

proposed.question: What should a child do if an adult touches them in a way that feels wrong?

options.text: Keep the secret so the adult is not upset
options.misconception: Believes that protecting an adult's feelings is more important than the child's safety.

options.text: Tell a trusted adult, like a parent or teacher
Wait quietly and hope it stops by itself
options.misconception: Believes that abuse will end on its own without any action.

options.text: Go with the adult to keep them company
options.misconception: Believes that a child should comply with any adult request, even a harmful one.

proposed.rationale: Telling a trusted adult is the way a child protects themselves from abuse and gets help.
proposed.excerpt: protect ourselves from child abuse

proposed.question: Which action best promotes child rights in our community?

options.text: Joining a campaign to teach others about children's rights
Keeping quiet about abuse to avoid trouble
options.misconception: Believes that silence protects children better than speaking out.

options.text: Punishing children who report abuse to adults
options.misconception: Believes that children who speak up about abuse deserve punishment.

options.text: Letting elders decide everything for children
options.misconception: Believes that children have no rights and that adults alone should decide for them.

proposed.rationale: Taking part in a campaign spreads awareness of children's rights and responsibilities in the community.
proposed.excerpt: participate in a campaign to promote child Rights and responsibilities in the community

proposed.question: Which is the best time to wash your hands?

options.text: After using the toilet
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing is only needed when hands look dirty.

options.text: Only on Sunday morning
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing is needed once a week rather than at key moments of the day.

options.text: Only before going to bed
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing matters only at night.

options.text: Only when visitors come home
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing is for guests and not for daily health.

proposed.rationale: Hands should be washed after using the toilet to prevent spreading germs that cause communicable diseases.
proposed.excerpt: hand washing, use of personal protective equipment, use of clean water and cleaning foods

proposed.question: Which of these helps to keep your body clean and healthy every day?

options.text: Wearing the same dirty clothes all week
options.misconception: Learner believes clothes do not affect body cleanliness if they look clean.

options.text: Bathing with clean water regularly
options.misconception: Learner believes bathing is correct and understood as a basic grooming practice.

options.text: Leaving nails long and uncut
options.misconception: Learner believes long nails are harmless to health and hygiene.

options.text: Eating food with unwashed hands
options.misconception: Learner believes eating without washing hands is harmless if the food is good.

proposed.rationale: Bathing with clean water regularly is a good grooming practice that keeps the body clean and healthy.
proposed.excerpt: use of clean water and cleaning foods

proposed.question: Why do we wear gumboots when we work on a wet shamba in Kenya?

options.text: To look smart when we walk to church
options.misconception: Learner believes protective gear is mainly for appearance and fashion.

options.text: To keep our feet safe from dirt and sharp objects
options.misconception: Learner believes protective gear is unnecessary when the work is outdoors.

options.text: To make our feet warm during the day
options.misconception: Learner believes protective equipment is only for weather comfort.

options.text: To run faster than our friends
options.misconception: Learner believes protective equipment is meant for sport or speed.

proposed.rationale: Gumboots are personal protective equipment that protect the feet from dirt, germs and injury.
proposed.excerpt: use of personal protective equipment

proposed.question: Ann is responsible for her own health. Which action shows she is taking charge of her body?

options.text: She waits for her mother to wash her face each morning
options.misconception: Learner believes personal grooming is someone else's job.

options.text: She brushes her teeth and combs her hair by herself each day
options.misconception: Learner believes self-care is the correct and responsible action.

options.text: She hides her dirty hands in her pockets
options.misconception: Learner believes hiding dirt solves the problem of dirty hands.

options.text: She skips washing because she feels tired
options.misconception: Learner believes tiredness is a valid reason to skip hygiene.

proposed.rationale: Brushing teeth and combing hair by herself shows responsibility and self-efficacy in good grooming.
proposed.excerpt: Demonstrate self -efficacy through practising good grooming ; and responsibility as they carry out health practices.

proposed.question: How does washing your hands properly help stop diseases from spreading in your home?

options.text: It removes germs that can cause sickness
options.misconception: Learner believes correct handwashing removes germs that spread disease.

options.text: It makes the hands smell nice for others
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing is mainly about smell and appearance.

options.text: It makes the skin lighter and softer
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing changes skin colour and beauty.

options.text: It keeps the hands warm in the cold morning
options.misconception: Learner believes handwashing is about temperature of the hands.

proposed.rationale: Handwashing removes germs, which prevents communicable diseases from spreading, a key link to good health.
proposed.excerpt: How does personal hygiene promote good health?

proposed.question: Why does our body need a balanced diet?

options.text: It helps us grow and stay healthy.
It makes us feel full for a long time only.
options.misconception: The learner thinks the main purpose of food is to fill the stomach rather than support growth and health.

options.text: It makes our food cheaper to buy each day.
options.misconception: The learner believes a balanced diet is mainly about saving money on food.

options.text: It lets us skip eating some meals in the day.
options.misconception: The learner thinks a balanced diet means eating less or missing meals.

proposed.rationale: A balanced diet gives the body the nutrients it needs to grow and stay healthy.
proposed.excerpt: explain importance of eating a balanced diet

proposed.question: What does a balanced diet mean?

options.text: Eating a variety of foods in the right amounts.
Eating only ugali and sukuma wiki every day.
options.misconception: The learner believes eating one filling local food every day is enough for good health.

options.text: Eating the same food that our friends eat.
options.misconception: The learner thinks a healthy diet is about copying others rather than choosing a mix of foods.

options.text: Eating as many sweets and snacks as we like.
options.misconception: The learner believes sweets and snacks can replace healthy foods.

proposed.rationale: A balanced diet includes many different foods in the correct proportions, which is what variety and proportion mean.
proposed.excerpt: importance of eating a balanced diet (variety and proportion)

proposed.question: Amina wants to make a balanced lunch with locally available foods. Which lunch is balanced?

options.text: Ugali, sukuma wiki, beans and a banana.
White rice and a cup of tea only.
options.misconception: The learner thinks any staple food with a drink makes a full meal.

options.text: Chips and a soda.
options.misconception: The learner believes fried fast foods and sugary drinks are healthy.

options.text: Mandazi and a glass of sugary juice.
options.misconception: The learner thinks a snack eaten with a sweet drink counts as a balanced lunch.

proposed.rationale: This lunch includes foods from several food groups: energy from ugali, vegetables from sukuma wiki, protein from beans, and fruit.
proposed.excerpt: Select foods from locally available foods that comprise a balanced diet

proposed.question: Which food group gives our body the most help to build and repair muscles?

options.text: Proteins such as beans, meat, fish and eggs.
Sugary foods such as sweets and cakes.
options.misconception: The learner believes sugar is the main nutrient for building the body.

options.text: Oils and fats used in cooking.
options.misconception: The learner thinks fats are the main body-building food.

options.text: Water in the glass we drink each day.
options.misconception: The learner believes drinking water alone builds body muscles.

proposed.rationale: Protein foods such as beans, meat, fish and eggs help the body build and repair muscles.
proposed.excerpt: Select food from different food-groups to make a balanced diet

proposed.question: Kamau's class is preparing a health talk. Why should they show a balanced meal together as a team?

options.text: To work together and encourage others to eat healthy foods.
To win a prize by making the biggest meal.
options.misconception: The learner believes the purpose of the presentation is competition and rewards.

options.text: To show that only one student knows about food.
options.misconception: The learner thinks group work is about one person doing everything.

options.text: To finish the class work quickly so they can go home.
options.misconception: The learner sees the presentation only as a way to finish early.

proposed.rationale: Working together in unity and promoting health awareness through class presentations is the purpose of collaborative balanced-meal presentations.
proposed.excerpt: Exhibit unity in making collaborative presentations of a balanced meal, and promote health awareness

proposed.question: A matatu has 14 seats. How many seats are in 3 matatus?

options.misconception: Adds the numbers together instead of multiplying them.
Rounds 14 up to 15 and then multiplies wrongly by 3.
Multiplies only the ones digit of 14 by 3 and ignores the tens digit.

proposed.rationale: Three matatus with 14 seats each have 14 times 3, which is 42 seats.
proposed.excerpt: multiply up to a 3 - digit number by up to a 2 - digit number

proposed.question: A farmer packs 125 eggs in each tray. He has 12 trays. How many eggs does he have in all?

options.misconception: Makes a carrying error when adding the partial products.
Multiplies by the tens digit of 12 only and leaves out the ones.
Adds the partial products wrongly, as if 12 were 10 plus 2 without the second part.

proposed.rationale: Multiplying 125 by 12 gives 1500, since 125 times 10 is 1250 and 125 times 2 is 250.
proposed.excerpt: work out multiplication of up to a 3 - digit number by up to a 2 - digit number

proposed.question: A shop sells 38 packets of sugar every day. About how many packets does it sell in 21 days, when you round each number to the nearest ten?

options.misconception: Rounds both numbers down to the lower ten instead of to the nearest ten.
Thinks an estimate must be the exact product, so works out the full multiplication.
Rounds to the nearest hundred instead of the nearest ten.

proposed.rationale: Rounding 38 to 40 and 21 to 20 gives 40 times 20, which is about 800.
proposed.excerpt: estimate product by rounding off numbers to the nearest ten

proposed.question: Wanjiru writes 2 times 5 equals 10, 4 times 5 equals 20 and 6 times 5 equals 30. What is the next product in her pattern?

options.misconception: Adds 5 to the last product, treating the pattern as adding the same factor each time.
Adds 20 to the last product, as if the step between products changes each time.
Thinks the next factor is 7 and multiplies 6 by 7, which is not the pattern used.

proposed.rationale: The next factor is 8, and 8 times 5 equals 40, which keeps the pattern of products going up by 10.
proposed.excerpt: create patterns involving multiplication of numbers with products not exceeding 100

proposed.question: A trader buys 27 crates of tomatoes. Each crate has 46 tomatoes. How many tomatoes does the trader have in all?

options.misconception: Multiplies only by the tens part of 46 and forgets the rest.
Makes a mistake when multiplying 27 by 6, so the second part is wrong.
Makes a small addition slip when putting the two parts together.

proposed.rationale: Multiplying 27 by 46 gives 1242, since 27 times 40 is 1080 and 27 times 6 is 162, and 1080 plus 162 is 1242.
proposed.excerpt: multiply up to a 3 - digit number by up to a 2 - digit number

proposed.question: What does a group of five tally marks look like?

options.text: Five upright lines placed side by side
options.misconception: Believes a tally group is five separate marks with no crossing line.

options.text: Four upright lines crossed by one slanting line
Three upright lines crossed by two slanting lines
options.misconception: Thinks the crossing line is drawn after three marks instead of four.

options.text: Four upright lines with one dot placed beside them
options.misconception: Thinks a dot can stand in for the fifth mark in a tally.

proposed.rationale: A group of five tally marks is four upright lines crossed by one slanting line, which makes counting in fives easy.
proposed.excerpt: draw tally marks of the collected and any data

proposed.question: A teacher wants to record the ages of 30 learners in her class. What should she draw first?

options.text: A list of every learner's name written in one line
options.misconception: Thinks a long written list is the best way to show how many learners share each age.

options.text: A drawing of one shoe for each learner in class
options.misconception: Thinks pictures alone are enough and that no table is needed.

options.text: A table with a column for each age and tally marks
A single sentence saying most learners are ten years old
options.misconception: Thinks one summary sentence records all the data without a table.

proposed.rationale: A table with a column for each age and tally marks records the data from real life clearly and in order.
proposed.excerpt: draw a table to record data from real life

proposed.question: Juma counted 12 learners who came to school by bus. What number should go in the frequency column for the bus row?

options.text: Two
options.misconception: Thinks the frequency is the number of tally groups, not the total count.

options.text: Five
options.misconception: Thinks the frequency is the size of one tally group.

options.text: Seven
options.misconception: Confuses the number of learners who came by bus with those who walked.

options.text: Twelve

proposed.rationale: The frequency is the total count of learners in that category, which is twelve.
proposed.excerpt: prepare a frequency table to represent data

proposed.question: A frequency table shows: Mango 14, Banana 9, Orange 6, Pawpaw 11. Which fruit was sold the least?

options.text: Mango
options.misconception: Thinks the first row in a table always shows the smallest value.

options.text: Banana
options.misconception: Confuses the second number in a table with the smallest number.

options.text: Orange
Pawpaw
options.misconception: Picks the fruit with the second-largest count, thinking it is the smallest.

proposed.rationale: Orange has the smallest frequency, 6, so it was sold the least.
proposed.excerpt: interpret data represented by frequency tables

proposed.question: A frequency table shows: Blue 8, Red 5, Green 8, Yellow 4. How many learners chose Red or Yellow altogether?

options.text: Nine
Eight
options.misconception: Takes the Blue or Green count and ignores the colours asked about.

options.text: Thirteen
options.misconception: Adds Blue and Red together and leaves out Yellow.

options.text: Five
options.misconception: Reads only the Red count and forgets to include Yellow.

proposed.rationale: Adding the Red count of 5 and the Yellow count of 4 gives 9 learners.
proposed.excerpt: interpret data represented by frequency tables

proposed.question: A metal spoon is left in a hot cup of tea. After a while, the handle of the spoon becomes hot. What is this way of heat moving through the spoon called?

options.text: Radiation
options.misconception: The learner thinks heat travels from the hot cup through the air to the handle.

options.text: Conduction
Convection
options.misconception: The learner thinks heat moves up the spoon with rising hot liquid or air.

options.text: Evaporation
options.misconception: The learner confuses heat moving along a material with water turning into vapour.

proposed.rationale: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a solid when particles pass energy to neighbouring particles, as happens along the metal spoon.
proposed.excerpt: demonstrate the modes of heat transfer in nature

proposed.question: Hot water at the bottom of a pot rises, and cooler water sinks to the bottom. What is this movement of heat called?

options.text: Convection
Conduction
options.misconception: The learner believes heat only moves when two solids touch each other.

options.text: Radiation
options.misconception: The learner believes heat travels in straight lines from the stove, like light.

options.text: Insulation
options.misconception: The learner confuses heat moving with stopping heat from escaping.

proposed.rationale: Convection happens in liquids and gases when warmer, less dense parts rise and cooler parts sink, creating a circulating movement.
proposed.excerpt: perform experiments to demonstrate the modes of heat transfer (conduction, convection and radiation)

proposed.question: We feel the warmth of the sun on our skin, even though the space between the sun and the earth is empty. Which mode of heat transfer does this show?

options.text: Conduction
options.misconception: The learner believes heat can only pass through a material that is touching the body.

options.text: Convection
options.misconception: The learner believes heat needs moving air to reach us.

options.text: Radiation
Friction
options.misconception: The learner thinks warmth comes only from rubbing or rough surfaces.

proposed.rationale: Radiation is heat that travels as waves through empty space, so it can warm us from the sun without any material between us.
proposed.excerpt: modes of heat transfer in nature

proposed.question: Which of these is a poor conductor of heat?

options.text: A wooden spoon
An iron frying pan
options.misconception: The learner believes all hard solid objects let heat pass through them easily.

options.text: A copper wire
options.misconception: The learner believes metal objects are the only things that can conduct heat.

options.text: An aluminium cup
options.misconception: The learner thinks a thin object always lets heat pass through quickly.

proposed.rationale: Wood does not let heat pass through it easily, so it is a poor conductor, while iron, copper and aluminium are good conductors.
proposed.excerpt: Classification of conductors of heat into good or poor conductors

proposed.question: Mama Akinyi needs to take a hot pot off the fire. Which thing should she use to hold the pot?

options.text: Her bare hands because she is quick
options.misconception: The learner thinks quick contact with a hot object is safe without any protection.

options.text: A wet cloth because water cools it
options.misconception: The learner believes water stops heat from burning the hands.

options.text: A dry cloth or an oven glove
A plastic bag because plastic is strong
options.misconception: The learner believes any strong material is safe to touch a hot object.

proposed.rationale: A dry cloth or oven glove protects the hands from heat, and a wet cloth can cause steam burns.
proposed.excerpt: Safety precautions when handling heat

proposed.question: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?

options.text: Sand and maize grains
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks any mixture of solids looks uniform, even when the parts can still be seen separately.

options.text: Salt dissolved in water
Beans mixed with small stones
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner believes a mixture is homogeneous whenever its parts are similar in size.

options.text: Soil mixed with pebbles
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks a mixture containing soil must be uniform throughout.

proposed.rationale: Salt dissolved in water is uniform throughout, so it is a homogeneous mixture.
proposed.excerpt: categorise mixtures as homogeneous (uniform) and heterogeneous (non- uniform)

proposed.question: Akinyi wants to remove small stones from a heap of maize grains. Which method should she use?

options.text: Using a magnet
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner believes a magnet can pick out any solid object, including stones and grains.

options.text: Boiling the mixture
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks heating is needed to separate solids from each other.

options.text: Picking stones out by hand
Pouring water over it
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks adding water will separate two dry solids.

proposed.rationale: Picking is a method that removes larger heterogeneous solids such as stones from grains by hand.
proposed.excerpt: Separating heterogeneous mixtures (Winnowing, picking, sieving, using magnet, Filtering, decanting, separating funnel)

proposed.question: Which method is best for removing iron nails from a heap of sand?

options.text: Using a magnet
Sieving through a fine mesh
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks sieving separates items by what they are made of, not only by size.

options.text: Winnowing with the wind
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner believes wind can blow heavy metal pieces away from sand.

options.text: Filtering through a cloth
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks filtering works to separate solid pieces from other solids.

proposed.rationale: A magnet attracts the iron nails, so they can be lifted out of the sand.
proposed.excerpt: using magnet

proposed.question: A farmer tosses maize into the air so the wind blows away the chaff. What method is this?

options.text: Sieving the grain
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks sieving is the only way to separate light and heavy parts of a mixture.

options.text: Decanting the water
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner believes decanting can separate solid grains from air.

options.text: Using a magnet
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks magnets can separate plant material from grain.

options.text: Winnowing the grain

proposed.rationale: Winnowing uses wind to blow the light chaff away from the heavier grains, which is a method used in agriculture.
proposed.excerpt: like straining milk, winnowing grains and straining honey

proposed.question: Which of these is a solid-liquid heterogeneous mixture?

options.text: Salt dissolved in water
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks any solid mixed with a liquid stays visible and is heterogeneous.

options.text: Sand stirred into water
Maize and beans in a sack
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner believes any mixture of solids is a solid-liquid mixture.

options.text: Oil floating on water
options.misconception: Choosing this suggests the learner thinks any mixture with water in it must be solid-liquid.

proposed.rationale: Sand stays separate from water and can be seen, so it is a solid-liquid heterogeneous mixture.
proposed.excerpt: Types of mixtures (heterogeneous and homogeneous) examples of (solid- solid, solid-liquid and liquid -liquid)

proposed.question: Which skill helps you find the main idea of a text quickly?

options.text: Skimming the text
Reading every word slowly
options.misconception: The learner believes the main idea can only be found by reading every word slowly from start to finish.

options.text: Copying the whole text
options.misconception: The learner believes that copying a text helps them understand its main idea.
